cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, glazing in all fixed and operable panels of swinging doors is considered a hazardous location, requiring safety glazing materials (BC §§ 2406.4, 2406.4.1). Exceptions include openings too small for a 3-inch sphere to pass through, decorative glazing, curved glazed panels in revolving doors, and commercial refrigerated-cabinet glazed doors. Thus, ordinary glazing in a swinging door is covered unless an exception applies.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and source citation match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, door-adjacent glazing within the 24-inch arc is hazardous when its bottom exposed edge is less than 60 inches above the walking surface. At 40 inches, it meets both conditions; on your stated premise that no exception applies, it is hazardous (BC § 2406.4.2).

cases.label: appropriate_clarification
cases.note: Correctly identifies individual-pane versus total-window area and supplies a supported conditional answer; matches pre-freeform source-audit addendum.
cases.answerText: **Conditionally yes:** the window is hazardous if the exposed area of an individual pane is greater than 9 square feet. The stated bottom (12 inches), top (60 inches), and walking-surface distance (24 inches) meet the other three thresholds; the code measures pane area, so the stated 12-square-foot window area alone does not establish that threshold. You state that no exception applies (2022 NYC BC § 2406.4.3).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and source citation match paired source key.
cases.answerText: Yes—if the glazing is in a wall, enclosure, or fence containing or facing a shower and its bottom exposed edge is less than 60 inches above a standing or walking surface, the hazardous-location rule applies to single glazing and **all panes in multiple glazing** (2022 NYC BC § 2406.4.5). The stated exception is limited to glazing more than 60 inches horizontally, in a straight line, from the water’s edge of a bathtub, hot tub, spa, whirlpool, or swimming pool; it does not name showers. The text therefore does not provide that exception for shower glazing.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and source citation match paired source key.
cases.answerText: Yes. At 40 inches above the landing, the glazing is less than 60 inches above it; if it is within the specified 60-inch horizontal arc of less than 180 degrees from the bottom tread nosing, it is a hazardous location, absent the stated exception (BC § 2406.4.7). The exception applies to glazing protected by a guard complying with Sections 1015 and 1607.8 where the glass plane is more than 18 inches from the guard.

cases.answerText: The required height cannot be determined from the supplied 2022 NYC enacted text: it contains no rule establishing how high a nonabsorbent wall surface must extend within 2 feet of a water closet. The supplied provisions address toilet-room use, fixtures, and water-closet compartments, not that surface-height requirement. (PC §§ 403.3, 405.3.4)

cases.answerText: For a 200-sf room, the 10-percent calculation is **20 sf of net glazed area** (200 × 0.10), under the 2022 NYC Building Code rule. But if the opening provides required natural light, the general rule also requires each such opening to have at least **12 sf** of glazed area; that minimum does not raise the 20-sf result. The Group R-3 exception also produces 20 sf here, because it requires the greater of 10 percent of room area or 12 sf. (BC § 1205.2.1)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and source citation match paired source key.
cases.answerText: The ordinary minimum is **8 feet (2438.4 mm) in any plan dimension** for a habitable space other than a kitchen (BC § 1208.1). Since you ask for the case with no exception, the listed exceptions to that minimum do not apply.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, a shower compartment must have both at least 900 square inches of interior cross-sectional area **and** a least dimension of at least 30 inches. The 30-inch minimum is measured from the finished interior dimension, excluding fixture valves, showerheads, soap dishes, and safety grab bars or rails. Thus, 950 square inches does not compensate for a 28-inch least dimension. (PC § 417.4)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, lavatories and group wash fixtures in public toilet facilities provided for customers, patrons, or visitors must deliver tempered water. Ordinarily it must be delivered through an approved temperature-limiting device conforming to ASSE 1070; where point-of-use heaters are installed, the outlet water temperature must instead be regulated to provide tempered water (PC § 416.5).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, urinals may replace no more than 50% of the required water closets in each bathroom or toilet room, so 60% exceeds the stated limit (PC § 419.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: A floor drain must have a drain outlet at least **3 inches (76 mm) in diameter** under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code (PC § 412.3).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: Yes. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, the room containing automatic clothes washers in a central washing facility of a multiple-family dwelling must have floor drains positioned to readily drain the entire floor area; each drain must have an outlet at least 3 inches in diameter and a lint strainer (PC § 412.4).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: No. Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, drainage piping may not decrease in size in the direction of flow; a 4-inch line reducing to 3 inches downstream is prohibited. The stated exception is a 4-inch-by-3-inch water-closet connection, which is not considered a size reduction (PC § 704.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Core rule, threshold or table entry matches paired source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** Under the 2022 NYC Plumbing Code, Table 706.3 marks a sanitary tee “–” for a horizontal-to-horizontal change in direction, so the table does not permit that use (PC § 706.3).

cases.answerText: For a lot 18 feet wide, an intake subject to MC § 401.4 must be located at the centerline between the lot lines; that item also states a minimum 10-foot distance from lot lines or buildings on the same lot. Group R-3 occupancies are excepted from § 401.4, and the occupancy is not specified, so whether that exception applies is unresolved.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** For an outdoor air intake in a residential occupancy, the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code limits screen openings to **1/2 inch maximum, measured in any direction**; 3/4-inch openings exceed that limit (MC § 401.5). If you mean a required outdoor air inlet serving a residential portion under the Fuel Gas Code, that provision specifies 1/4-inch openings (FGC § 618.5).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **No.** The outdoor air required by the applicable ventilation rate may not be recirculated; only air supplied in excess of that requirement is generally eligible for recirculation (MC § 403.2.1). The code separately allows the minimum required outdoor-air rate to be reduced if a registered design professional demonstrates an engineered ventilation system designed under the ASHRAE 62.1 Indoor Air Quality Procedure; that is a reduction in the required outdoor-air rate, not permission to replace it with recirculated air (MC § 403.2). Exceptions restrict recirculation further in specified spaces, including certain spaces requiring mechanical exhaust.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **Yes—in principle.** The 2022 NYC Mechanical Code expressly allows air transferred from occupiable spaces to serve as makeup air for required exhaust systems, including baths, provided the transfer-air and exhaust quantities meet the applicable rates and required outdoor air is supplied directly to the bathroom, to the space(s) supplying the transfer air, or to both (MC § 403.2.2; § 403.3.1.1). The exception bars transfer from a source space when recirculation from that source space is prohibited; it does not, by itself, bar transfer air *into* a bathroom. The table lists exhaust rates for bathrooms and toilet rooms and marks the row “g,” which requires mechanical exhaust and prohibits recirculation from those spaces (MC § 403.3.1.1, Note g; § 403.2.1, Item 4).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: Intermittent mechanical ventilation in an enclosed parking garage must operate automatically using **carbon monoxide detectors together with nitrogen dioxide detectors**. The system must operate when it detects **25 ppm carbon monoxide or 500 ppb nitrogen dioxide**; install the detectors according to their manufacturers’ instructions (2022 NYC Mechanical Code § 404.1).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: Automatic operation may reduce garage ventilation only to **0.05 cfm per square foot of floor area**; the system must also be capable of providing **0.75 cfm per square foot** (2022 NYC Mechanical Code § 404.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Governing rule, threshold and relevant qualifiers match paired source key.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Mechanical Code, an installation exhausting 250 cfm exceeds the 200-cfm threshold and must be provided with makeup air. If the dryer is designed for installation in a closet, the code also specifies an opening of at least 100 square inches in the closet enclosure **or** makeup air by other approved means. (MC § 504.6)

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and governing source match paired key, including applicable scope qualifications.
cases.answerText: Generally, ducts permitted through a fire wall must have **listed fire dampers and smoke dampers**, installed according to their listing (MC § 607.5.1; BC § 717.5.1). Such penetrations are allowed only through fire walls **not on a lot line**, and must comply with BC § 717 and the applicable opening limits (BC § 706.11). The two supplied smoke-damper exceptions differ; omitting the smoke damper is supported only if the conditions in both provisions are met, including the Mechanical Code’s standby-power condition and the Building Code’s continuous-monitoring and maintenance conditions.

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and governing source match paired key, including applicable scope qualifications.
cases.answerText: **No—not by itself.** The 2022 NYC Mechanical Code says ducts and air-transfer openings may not penetrate interior exit stairway enclosures except as permitted by Building Code § 1023.5; installing a fire damper does not itself establish that exception. Whether a particular penetration is permitted under § 1023.5 cannot be determined from the supplied text because that section is not included (MC § 607.5.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and governing source match paired key, including applicable scope qualifications.
cases.answerText: **No—not under the general direct-vent exception.** FGC § 303.3 prohibits appliances in sleeping rooms, and its direct-vent exception applies only to rooms “other than those used for sleeping purposes.” (FGC § 303.3) A separate, narrow provision deems a gas-fired direct-vent space-heating appliance used to heat a sleeping room to be outside the room, but only if it complies with all requirements in §§ 303.3.1.1–303.3.1.7. (FGC § 303.3.1) The supplied text establishes some of those requirements, but not all seven; therefore, it does not establish whether a particular appliance qualifies for that separate provision.

cases.answerText: The minimum dimension of an outdoor combustion-air opening is **3 inches (76.2 mm)** under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code. This is the minimum dimension, not the required free-area calculation; the applicable opening method also sets free-area requirements, and the opening size must comply with any applicable NYC Department of Environmental Protection rules (FGC §§ 304.6, 304.6.1–304.6.2).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and governing source match paired key, including applicable scope qualifications.
cases.answerText: **Yes.** Under the 2022 NYC Fuel Gas Code, fittings in concealed locations are limited to threaded elbows, tees and couplings, or welded fittings; threaded elbows are expressly included (FGC § 404.5). This answers whether that fitting type is permitted, not whether a particular installation complies with other location restrictions, including the separate prohibited-locations rule (FGC § 404.3).

cases.label: correct_useful
cases.note: Conclusion and governing source match paired key, including applicable scope qualifications.
cases.answerText: For underground gas piping passing below grade through a building’s outer foundation or basement wall, the protective sleeve must extend at least **1 inch beyond the inside face** and **4 inches beyond the outside face** of the foundation wall. The code allows a different extension “as otherwise required by the gas provider.” The annular space between the pipe and sleeve must also be waterproofed and sealed (2022 NYC FGC § 404.6).

The conduit must be protected against corrosion and installed under one of the three specified configurations in §§ 404.14.1–404.14.3 (FGC § 404.14).

cases.answerText: **No—not under the supplied 2022 NYC Construction Code text.** The Mechanical Code assumes no smoking for its baseline ventilation rates, but if smoking is anticipated in a space other than a non-tobacco hookah establishment, it requires ventilation beyond the table rates in accordance with accepted engineering practice; that is a ventilation condition, not a smoking prohibition (MC § 403.3.1.1). The supplied Building Code smoking ban is limited to construction and demolition sites (BC § 3303.7.3). This answers only what the supplied Construction Code provisions establish; it does not determine whether another law prohibits smoking.

cases.answerText: **The supplied 2022 NYC Building Code evidence does not determine whether highly combustible display goods may be placed 3 feet from an exterior exit door.** It requires at least one exterior door meeting BC § 1010.1.1 (BC § 1022.2), and the supplied cross-reference describes that section as addressing door-opening width and height. cases.answerText: The sign must say “SHAFTWAY” in **red letters at least 6 inches (152.4 mm) high, on a white background**. It applies to an outside opening accessible to the Fire Department that opens directly onto a hoistway or shaftway communicating between two or more floors; place the sign so it is readily discernible from outside the building (BC § 914.1.1).

cases.answerText: Under the 2022 NYC Building Code, address characters generally must be at least **4 inches high** and **0.5 inch wide**. However, the borough president’s rules may provide otherwise, and the supplied evidence does not include the applicable borough rules. (BC § 501.2)

cases.answerText: The owner must ensure that the key kept in the key box is replaced whenever a lock securing the area, box, or cabinet is changed or rekeyed (2022 NYC Fire Code § 506.2.2).

cases.answerText: **No.** Stored boxes may not impede the required access to a sprinkler valve that is a full-open valve or shutoff valve. The 2022 NYC Plumbing Code requires access to all valves in those categories (PC § 606.3).
